passage: At two, Baljeet sat on the balcony floor with a fat crayon, dragging red lines across a sheet of paper and then over the tiles. His mother Alka did not ask what it was. She said, "You are working so hard! Look at those big swirls." Baljeet beamed and pressed even harder. At ten, he folded a paper boat for his grandfather's birthday, and spent an evening getting the sharp creases right. Alka looked at it and said, "You matched the corners so neatly, and the blue paper is a lovely choice." Baljeet held it a little higher. His grandfather sailed it in the sink, delighted. At twenty, Baljeet made a short film for his design course about an old man closing his shop for the last time. He wanted it to say that endings can be gentle. At the screening, his friend Joseph said afterwards, "It made me so sad. The empty shelves at the end were heartbreaking." Baljeet blinked. He had wanted people to feel calm. Later he asked two other viewers what they saw, and their answers were different again, which puzzled and interested him.

qa.q: What did Baljeet fold for his grandfather's birthday?
qa.a: He folded a paper boat.

qa.q: How do the responses to Baljeet's work matter at two, ten and twenty?
qa.a: At two his mother praised his effort and swirls rather than asking what it was, at ten she named the neat corners and lovely blue paper, and at twenty Joseph read the film as sad when Baljeet meant it as gentle. Specific words support him, while strangers bring their own feelings to what he makes.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when Joseph called the film heartbreaking?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a bit puzzled, because he had meant viewers to feel calm.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do to learn how his film comes across?
qa.a: He could keep asking different viewers what they saw and felt, and listen without arguing.

grounding: One person's making at three ages: scribbling for the joy of marks, a folded boat given with care, and a short film whose audience reads it differently from the maker's intent.

passage: On the second afternoon of the holidays, nine-year-old Devika flopped on the sofa and groaned, "I'm so bored." Her mother Ankita said only, "Mm," and carried on chopping. Devika sighed for a whole quarter of an hour. Then she looked at the cushions, the stool and the old blanket, and began to build a fort. By evening it had rooms, a shop and a password. At twenty, Devika opened her admission letter to the college she had dreamed of for years and felt strangely empty. The chase was over, and so was the direction it had given her. Her friend Noor asked why she was so quiet. "I got everything I wanted," Devika said. "So why do I feel nothing?" At twenty-five, she worked at a firm with the same commute, the same lift and the same tasks. She was not sad. She was grey. Most evenings she watched videos until midnight without choosing any. Noor, now her colleague, said, "When did anything last surprise you?" Devika thought about the fort and could not answer.

qa.q: What did Devika build on the holiday afternoon?
qa.a: She built a fort.

qa.q: How do Devika's flat feelings at nine, twenty and twenty-five relate to one another?
qa.a: At nine boredom led her to invent a fort once nobody hurried to fill it, at twenty getting into her dream college left her strangely empty because the chase that gave direction was over, and at twenty-five the same commute and tasks left her grey and drifting to videos. Emptiness at first opened the door to imagination, but later it sat without a new direction.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when she asked why she felt nothing after getting what she wanted?
qa.a: She felt hollow and confused, missing the sense of direction her goal had given her.

qa.q: What could Devika try to bring some direction back into her routine?
qa.a: She could pick a small project she cares about, like a course or a new hobby, and set aside a regular hour for it instead of aimless videos.

grounding: The same person meets ennui at three ages: restless boredom that turns into play, flatness after reaching a big goal, and the greyness of a routine job.

passage: At five, Darshan's mother Zeenat put one sweet on the table. "If you can wait until I finish my tea, you can have two." Darshan looked at the sweet, then at her cup. He picked up the one sweet and ate it fast. Two would have been better, but later was too far away to picture. At fifteen, his friend Yash messaged him with a game challenge one evening before a science test three months away. Darshan wanted a better grade, but an hour of gaming was vivid and the grade was faint. "Just one match," he typed, and played until eleven. At twenty, Darshan got his monthly stipend and spent most of it that weekend on new headphones and dinners out. He knew he would want savings for the trip in spring. "Next month I'll be strict," he told Yash on the balcony. Next month the same thing happened. Yash raised an eyebrow. "Didn't you say that in August?" Darshan laughed and looked down, aware that he had.

qa.q: How many sweets could Darshan have if he waited?
qa.a: He could have two sweets if he waited until his mother finished her tea.

qa.q: How does Darshan's choice of now over later repeat at five, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At five he ate one sweet fast rather than wait for two, at fifteen he played a match instead of studying for a grade months away, and at twenty he spent his stipend at once though he wanted savings for the trip. Each time the reward in front of him felt bigger than the better one later.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when Yash reminded him about August?
qa.a: He felt sheepish and a bit guilty, because he knew he had said the same thing before.

qa.q: What could Darshan try so that next month does not repeat this month?
qa.a: He could move a fixed part of his stipend into savings on the day it arrives, so he does not have to decide in the moment.

grounding: The same person prefers the reward in front of him at three ages: one sweet now, an hour of gaming, and spending a stipend at once.

passage: At ten, Yogesh sat in the back seat of the car on a hot morning, and saw his classmate Suraj walking the long road to school, his bag heavy. Yogesh had never thought about how Suraj got there before. At school, he learned that Suraj also read by a streetlamp, since there was no quiet room at home. Yogesh felt strange, sometimes guilty, sometimes curious, and a little annoyed that no one had told him. He asked his father at dinner, "Why do some people have to walk so far?" His father didn't answer at once. At fifteen, Yogesh came top in mathematics. His cousin Joseph said, jokingly, "Well, you've always had it easier, with your own room and tutors." Yogesh's face went hot. "I worked hard! Nobody handed me anything." Joseph shrugged and changed the subject. That night Yogesh lay awake and thought of Suraj on the road, and how his own work and his own room were both real. He felt confused and did not know what to do with it.

qa.q: What did Suraj do by the streetlamp?
qa.a: Suraj read by a streetlamp.

qa.q: How is Yogesh's reaction to the difference in starting points different at ten and at fifteen?
qa.a: At ten he noticed Suraj's long walk and lack of a quiet room and felt curious, guilty and annoyed, and asked why. At fifteen, when Joseph said he had it easier, he felt attacked and said he worked hard. Later he saw that his work and his advantages were both real.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when Joseph said he had always had it easier?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defensive, and his hot face shows he heard it as an attack on his effort.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do with what he has learned about Suraj's situation?
qa.a: He could ask Suraj, kindly and without pity, what would help, and share what he has, like a quiet corner or books.

grounding: The same person notices unequal starting points at two ages: curiosity and guilt at ten, and defensiveness at fifteen when reminded of his advantages.

passage: At two, Parveen watched bright, fast cartoons on the tablet every night after dinner. By bedtime her cheeks were flushed, she kicked the blanket and cried for another one. Her father Jomon switched the screen off and read her a picture book in the dim room, and after a few nights of quiet play and books, she settled sooner. At fifteen, Parveen lay in bed scrolling. "One more video," she told herself, and then another, afraid she would miss something in the group chat. It was past midnight when she put the phone down, and she still lay awake, with her mind buzzing. The next day she was snappy and everything seemed heavy. At twenty-five, she answered emails from her bed at eleven at night. Afterwards her head kept running through tomorrow's tasks and she woke unrested. Her friend Nandini said, "Try closing the laptop at nine and doing nothing with a screen for half an hour." Parveen tried a week of it. She kept a paperback on the pillow, and her mind began to slow by ten.

qa.q: What did Parveen's father do when he switched the screen off?
qa.a: He read her a picture book in the dim room.

qa.q: How do screens affect Parveen's sleep at two, fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: At two bright, fast cartoons left her wired and crying, at fifteen scrolling and fear of missing out kept her awake and snappy, and at twenty-five late emails kept her mind buzzing. In each case the screen before bed delayed her settling, and a screen-free wind-down helped.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when she kept scrolling one more video at fifteen?
qa.a: She felt anxious about missing something in the group chat, so she kept going even when tired.

qa.q: What could Parveen do to keep her evenings calm on busy work days?
qa.a: She could set a time to close her laptop, keep the phone out of the bed, and use a book or quiet music for the last half hour.

grounding: The same person's sleep is affected by screens at three ages: fast cartoons at two, phone scrolling at fifteen, and late emails at twenty-five.

passage: In his first month at the company, Sumit noticed that the written rules said nothing about whom to include on emails or when to speak in meetings. He watched. He saw that his manager liked to be told first, and that nobody interrupted the director. He was anxious about making a wrong move, so he asked his mentor Rafiq quietly at the tea counter, "Is there something I should know that isn't written down?" Rafiq laughed and told him. At twenty-five, Sumit wanted a promotion. He had coffee with senior people, praised colleagues' good work, and joined the planning committee, all of which was normal. Then, before a review, he left a colleague, Pankaj, off an email chain so the manager would see only Sumit's part of the project, and did not mention a delay that was his. Rafiq noticed and found him afterwards. "Promotions are fine to want," Rafiq said. "But leaving out Pankaj and hiding the delay is a slip." Sumit went pale. That afternoon he sent the full email and told the manager about the delay himself.

qa.q: Who did Sumit ask at the tea counter?
qa.a: He asked his mentor Rafiq.

qa.q: How does Sumit's learning of unwritten rules at his first job relate to his behaviour at twenty-five?
qa.a: In the first month he watched to learn the unwritten rules, like whom to include on emails and when to speak, and at twenty-five he used that knowledge to build allies and shape impressions. Coffee with seniors and praising others was normal, but leaving Pankaj off the email and hiding the delay was harmful.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when he asked Rafiq if there was something not written down?
qa.a: He felt anxious and afraid of missteps, so he sought help quietly.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that helped, and what more could Sumit do to repair things with Pankaj?
qa.a: Rafiq spoke to Sumit directly and clearly, and Sumit could tell Pankaj what happened and apologise for leaving Pankaj off.

grounding: The same person moves from learning an office's unwritten rules as a new graduate to using them for advantage at twenty-five, first through normal networking and then by undermining a colleague and hiding a delay.
